svg.title: Agent with tools versus the pipeline we built
svg.desc: Left: an agent with board tools. The model calls get_board, find_equipment, update_card twice and create_card, one turn at a time, and the whole conversation is re-sent every turn, so the context bar grows to six turns. Right: the pipeline we built. The model extracts what was said and links names and machines, code pulls the matching cards from the board, the model picks the card and says why, and fixed rules write the change. Always three model calls per stand-up; 97% of updates right at $0.007 per stand-up.

g.text: An agent would fetch the board with a tool call. But we know what it needs before it starts, so plain code can load it.
The model decides what to fetch, one tool call at a time.
More turns, more tokens, and it can take a different path each run.
Harder to test step by step.
Code loads what the model needs. The model only reads and picks.
every job, new or update, with who and which machine
every job, new or update, with who and which machine
pick from a shortlist: “the Atlas” → Air Compressor 1
pick from a shortlist: “the Atlas” → Air Compressor 1
that person's open cards + same machine · about 4 cards
that person's open cards + same machine · about 4 cards
Pick the card, and say why
same job, or none of them
Pick the card, and say why
same job, or none of them
create · update · ignore (an update never creates)
create · update · ignore (an update never creates)
Same information either way. Loading it in code means fewer calls, the same steps every run, and every step scored on its own.
An agent earns its keep when it can't know up front what to fetch: open questions, lots of systems, or needing to ask a person.
